newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Britain pushing U.N. resolution to condemn Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Britain pushing U.N. resolution to condemn Iraq.

text.p: Despite unanimity on maintaining sanctions against Iraq, the U.N. Security Council had trouble in responding to Baghdad's offensive in Kurdish areas that prompted two U.S. cruise missile attacks.

Britain produced a draft resolution on Tuesday condemning Iraq for its actions and demanding it pull out its troops from the northern Kurdish region immediately. The measure could be adopted this week, after revisions.
But absent in the resolution was any mention of the U.S. attacks, a recognition of a divided world on their legitimacy.
"If we were to include that issue, there would be absolutely no common view," said one senior French official.

The United States fired 37 Tomahawk cruise missiles on Tuesday morning and unleashed another 17 early on Wednesday morning, Iraqi time, to punish Baghdad's incursions into restricted Kurdish provinces.

At Tuesday's sesssion, U.S. deputy ambassador Edward Gnehm, a Middle East expert, said it was necessary to condemn Iraq's action because its troops rained down one shell every six seconds on civilians in the northern city of Arbil.
"There are already widespread reports of mass executions, detentions, looting and house to house searches by the secret police," in Arbil, he said.

Before discussing the Kurdish crisis, the council, as expected, retained intact the stiff economic sanctions imposed on Baghdad since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait at a meeting scheduled before the latest crisis.

An exemption to the sanctions is the oil-for-food deal, which allows limited Iraqi oil sales so it can supply its people with food and medicine. The plan is on hold now, depending on what happens in the north.
The British proposal asks the U.N. Secretary-General to report urgently on the implications of Iraq's behavior on implementing the oil-for-food deal. It also:
-- condemns attacks by Iraqi armed forces against the Kurds
-- demands Baghdad withdraw its troops
-- calls on Iran to stop its miitary actions in the north
-- calls on rival Kurdish action to resume talks.
But France, Russia, China, Egypt and other states initially opposed the draft, although diplomats said they tempered their comments during the council discussions.
"There was general assent that Iraq's actions last week had broken the status quo, which has existed in that part of iraq for a considerable time," said Britain's deputy ambassador Stephen Gomersall.
"There was also general agreement that withdrawal by iraqi troops will be an essential element to any return of the status quo," he told reporters.

However, Russia's ambassador Sergei Larvov, who introduced a rival milder document, said: "We believe that the only thing the Security Council can do under the circumstances is to express its serious concern at what has happened and to call on all parties to refrain from the use of force."

But France and others contended that Iraq's invasion of its own territory to aid the Kurdish Democratic Party against the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, which is close to Iran, did not necessarily violate U.N. resolutions.

Nevertheless resolution 688, adopted on April 5, 1991 at the instigation of the late French President Francois Mitterrand, condemns Iraq's "repression" against minorities and demands Baghdad allow humanitarian relief in the area.

The United States has also used the resolution to justify its military attacks but the document deliberately avoided authorizing the use of force. It also does not set up exclusion zones, which were imposed by the United States, Britain and France outside of the United Nations.
But in the aftermath of the Gulf War, the allied efforts were applauded in helping Kurds, who fled Iraqi troops over stark mountains in bitter weather.
